blocks.text: Peripheral arterial disease is usually caused by atherosclerotic narrowing or occlusion of arteries supplying the lower limbs. It increases the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, tissue loss and amputation.

Treatment has two complementary aims: reduce cardiovascular and limb events through preventive medication, and preserve limb function through symptom treatment, wound care and revascularisation when indicated.

The 2024 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline distinguishes asymptomatic PAD, chronic symptomatic PAD, chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) and acute limb ischaemia (ALI). These categories require different treatment pathways.

Emergency warning: Sudden limb pain with a cold or pale limb, absent pulses, sensory loss or weakness may indicate acute limb ischaemia. Arrange emergency vascular assessment immediately. Do not delay referral while trying oral medication or outpatient tests.

rows: Asymptomatic PAD
Objective arterial disease without recognised symptoms
Cardiovascular risk reduction and preventive foot care
Chronic symptomatic PAD
Stable exertional leg symptoms, including intermittent claudication
Antiplatelet/antithrombotic strategy when indicated, high-intensity statin, structured exercise and symptom treatment
Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI)
Persistent ischaemic rest pain, non-healing ulceration or gangrene
Urgent vascular assessment, wound care, infection management and revascularisation assessment
Acute limb ischaemia (ALI)
Sudden reduction in limb perfusion, generally developing over hours to days
Emergency anticoagulation when appropriate and urgent revascularisation assessment

items.text: Prevent myocardial infarction, stroke and vascular death.
Reduce major adverse limb events and recurrent ischaemia.
Improve walking distance and quality of life.
Promote wound healing and preserve the limb.
Treat acute arterial occlusion rapidly enough to prevent irreversible tissue injury.

blocks.text: For symptomatic PAD, single antiplatelet therapy is recommended to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events. Common options are clopidogrel or aspirin.
**Option 1** — Clopidogrel
Example prescription
Clopidogrel 75 mg tablets
Take one tablet orally once daily.
Quantity: 30 tablets.
Review bleeding risk, previous adverse effects, concurrent anticoagulants and relevant drug interactions.
**Option 2** — Aspirin
Example prescription
Aspirin 75–100 mg orally once daily, using the locally available strength and formulation.
Quantity: 30 tablets.
Review gastrointestinal bleeding risk, allergy, concurrent NSAIDs and any other antithrombotic medicines.
**Important precautions**

items.text: Do not routinely combine aspirin and clopidogrel long term for stable PAD without a specific indication.
Check for active bleeding, previous major gastrointestinal bleeding, thrombocytopenia and other medicines that increase bleeding risk.
Following a recent endovascular procedure or stent, a specialist may prescribe dual antiplatelet therapy for a defined period.

blocks.text: PAD is established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, so high-intensity statin therapy is generally indicated unless contraindicated or not tolerated.

items.text: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg orally once daily.
Rosuvastatin 20–40 mg orally once daily, when appropriate.

blocks.text: The aim is a substantial LDL-C reduction—commonly at least 50%. If LDL-C remains above the applicable threshold despite maximally tolerated statin therapy, consider adding ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor according to risk, availability and the relevant guideline.

**Monitoring:** Check baseline liver transaminases, review interactions and assess lipid response after initiation or dose adjustment. Investigate significant muscle pain or weakness; measure CK when clinically indicated.

For selected patients with symptomatic PAD, including those after lower-extremity revascularisation, the combination of vascular-dose rivaroxaban and low-dose aspirin reduces cardiovascular and limb events. It also increases major bleeding risk, so suitability must be assessed individually.
Example prescription for an eligible adult

items.text: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily.
Aspirin 75–100 mg orally once daily, or the locally recommended low-dose regimen.

blocks.text: This is a vascular-protection regimen, not a therapeutic dose for acute DVT, pulmonary embolism or atrial fibrillation.
Avoid or seek specialist review in active bleeding, high bleeding risk, significant renal or hepatic disease, or when another anticoagulation regimen is required.
Do not use full-intensity oral anticoagulation solely to prevent cardiovascular or limb events in PAD when there is no separate indication, such as atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism.

content_groups.group_title: D. Blood pressure and diabetes treatment

items.text: Treat hypertension using an appropriate antihypertensive regimen; an ACE inhibitor or ARB is often useful when indicated.
In patients with type 2 diabetes and PAD, consider an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit when appropriate.
Individualise treatment for renal function, heart failure, frailty, hypoglycaemia risk and other contraindications.
Smoking cessation, foot care, exercise and dietary management remain essential components of treatment.

blocks.text: Structured exercise is a core treatment for chronic symptomatic PAD. Revascularisation is considered when symptoms remain functionally limiting despite appropriate medical treatment and exercise, and when the expected benefit justifies procedural risk.
Cilostazol can improve claudication symptoms and walking distance. It is contraindicated in heart failure of any severity.
**Example prescription**
Cilostazol 100 mg tablets
Take one tablet orally twice daily, at least 30 minutes before or 2 hours after breakfast and dinner, according to product instructions.
Quantity: 60 tablets for 30 days.
Avoid in any patient with heart failure. Review bleeding risk, interacting medicines, palpitations and other contraindications before prescribing.
**Adverse effects**: Headache, diarrhoea, dizziness and palpitations. Reassess tolerability after 2–4 weeks and functional benefit over the following 3–6 months.
Avoid or review carefully: Heart failure, bleeding risk, and strong CYP3A4 or CYP2C19 inhibitors that may increase drug exposure. Follow the product label for dose adjustments.

items.text: Offer supervised exercise therapy where available, or a structured community/home-based programme with behavioural support.
A typical supervised programme uses repeated walking intervals, with rest when moderate claudication occurs, progressing over multiple sessions.
Encourage regular adherence rather than occasional strenuous exercise.
In patients with foot ulceration, rest pain or CLTI, exercise advice must be adapted to avoid tissue injury and must not delay vascular assessment.

blocks.text: Pentoxifylline is not recommended as a routine treatment for claudication because meaningful benefit has not been established.
CLTI involves advanced arterial insufficiency, often with ischaemic rest pain, non-healing ulcers or gangrene. Treatment is limb-preserving and usually requires a vascular team.

items.text: Urgent vascular referral to assess revascularisation options.
Antiplatelet and intensive lipid-lowering therapy, if appropriate.
Wound care, pressure offloading and infection treatment.
Optimisation of diabetes, nutrition, renal function and other comorbidities.
Analgesia tailored to the patient's pain and comorbidities.
Assessment for revascularisation by endovascular, surgical or hybrid approaches.

blocks.text: Antibiotics: Do not prescribe antibiotics solely because an ischaemic ulcer is present. Use them when clinical infection is suspected or established, selecting the regimen according to severity, likely pathogens, local resistance and culture results where appropriate.
Do not delay revascularisation assessment while waiting for an ulcer to fail prolonged wound care or antibiotic treatment.
Acute limb ischaemia can rapidly cause irreversible nerve and muscle injury. The limb must be assessed urgently for viability and the need for immediate revascularisation.

Unless contraindicated, IV unfractionated heparin is commonly given promptly when ALI is diagnosed, while urgent vascular assessment and revascularisation planning proceed. UFH limits thrombus propagation but does not replace revascularisation.
**Example treatment framework**

items.text: Start IV UFH according to the hospital's weight-based acute limb ischaemia protocol.
Use the specified bolus and infusion regimen, with aPTT or anti-Xa monitoring as directed.
Check bleeding risk, platelet count, renal function and possible HIT.
Avoid UFH when there is a contraindication such as active major bleeding, and seek specialist advice.

blocks.text: I am not providing a universal bolus/infusion prescription here because the correct protocol depends on the patient's weight, bleeding risk, the likely cause and the planned procedure. Use the institution's emergency vascular anticoagulation protocol.

blocks.title: Depending on limb viability, anatomy, cause and local expertise, options include:

items.text: Surgical embolectomy or thrombectomy.
Catheter-directed thrombolysis in selected patients.
Endovascular thrombectomy or angioplasty.
Bypass surgery or hybrid intervention.
Amputation when tissue is irreversibly damaged or the limb is not salvageable.

blocks.text: Systemic thrombolysis is not a routine substitute for urgent vascular assessment and a tailored revascularisation plan.

content_groups.group_title: C. Pain relief and supportive care

blocks.text: Provide appropriate analgesia, protect the limb from pressure and trauma, and correct relevant physiological abnormalities. Avoid tight compression, extreme heating or cooling, and unnecessary manipulation of an acutely ischaemic limb.
Immediate escalation is particularly important if there is new sensory loss, weakness or paralysis, as these can indicate a threatened or immediately threatened limb.
Revascularisation is considered when symptoms remain limiting despite appropriate medical treatment, or when CLTI makes limb preservation a priority.

rows: Endovascular angioplasty/stenting
Selected arterial lesions, often with lower procedural burden
Surgical bypass
Selected patients with suitable anatomy, conduit and operative fitness
Hybrid intervention
Combined open and endovascular treatment for complex disease
Amputation
Irreversible tissue damage, a non-salvageable limb or selected cases where salvage is not feasible

blocks.text: The choice depends on arterial anatomy, lesion length, wound severity, infection, available conduit, comorbidities, expected durability and patient preferences. Revascularisation should be planned by a vascular specialist team.

items.text: Antiplatelet therapy is recommended after endovascular or surgical revascularisation.
Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin is recommended for suitable patients to reduce major cardiovascular and limb events.
After endovascular revascularisation, dual antiplatelet therapy may be reasonable for approximately 1–6 months, depending on the intervention and bleeding risk.
If full-dose anticoagulation is needed for another condition, such as AF or VTE, additional antiplatelet therapy should be individualised to minimise bleeding risk.

rows: Aspirin
Gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, hypersensitivity
Clopidogrel
Bleeding, rare thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura; interactions with some CYP2C19 inhibitors
Rivaroxaban plus aspirin
Increased bleeding; assess renal/hepatic function and interacting medicines
Atorvastatin/rosuvastatin
Myalgia, myopathy, rare rhabdomyolysis; interactions and liver disease
Cilostazol
Headache, diarrhoea, palpitations; contraindicated in any heart failure
UFH
Bleeding, HIT and thrombocytopenia
Thrombolytic agents
Major bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage
Furosemide, when used for comorbid heart failure
Dehydration, electrolyte disturbances and renal dysfunction

items.text: Anticoagulant plus dual antiplatelet therapy can substantially increase bleeding.
Rivaroxaban and aspirin should not be added to full-dose anticoagulation without a clear indication and specialist review.
NSAIDs can increase bleeding when combined with antiplatelets or anticoagulants.
Statin interactions may increase myopathy risk; review macrolides, azole antifungals and other interacting medicines.
Cilostazol should not be prescribed in heart failure, regardless of ejection fraction.

rows: After starting preventive therapy
Adherence, bleeding risk, interactions and tolerance
4–12 weeks after statin initiation or dose change
Lipid response, adverse effects and need for additional therapy
During claudication treatment
Walking ability, quality of life, cilostazol tolerance if used
After revascularisation
Limb perfusion, wound healing, antithrombotic regimen and signs of restenosis
During CLTI wound care
Wound progress, infection, pressure offloading, glycaemic control and vascular plan
Long-term
Cardiovascular risk factors, smoking status, foot care, renal function when relevant and recurrent limb symptoms

blocks.text: New rest pain, a non-healing wound, gangrene or a sudden change in limb symptoms requires urgent reassessment rather than waiting for routine follow-up.

items.text: Inspect the feet regularly, especially in diabetes or neuropathy.
Wear well-fitting footwear and avoid walking barefoot.
Avoid treating corns, calluses or ulcers with caustic preparations or unqualified procedures.
Seek prompt assessment for a new ulcer, infection, colour change or wound that is not healing.
Stop smoking and maintain regular follow-up.
Take prescribed preventive medicines consistently.
Follow the structured exercise plan if there is no CLTI or other contraindication.
Know the emergency symptoms of acute limb ischaemia and seek immediate care if they occur.
Using full-dose anticoagulation solely for stable PAD when there is no separate indication.
Prescribing cilostazol to a patient with heart failure.
Adding rivaroxaban to aspirin without assessing bleeding risk.
Continuing dual antiplatelet therapy indefinitely after a procedure without a defined indication.
Treating an ischaemic ulcer with antibiotics alone while delaying vascular assessment.
Treating acute limb ischaemia with outpatient medication rather than emergency referral.
Failing to prescribe high-intensity statin therapy or review LDL-C response.
Overlooking foot care, smoking cessation and structured exercise as essential parts of treatment.
Symptomatic PAD requires cardiovascular risk reduction and antiplatelet or appropriate antithrombotic treatment.
High-intensity statin therapy is a cornerstone of PAD management.
Clopidogrel 75 mg daily or low-dose aspirin are common single-antiplatelet options.
Low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin can reduce cardiovascular and limb events in appropriately selected patients, at the cost of increased bleeding.
Cilostazol can improve claudication but is contraindicated in heart failure.
CLTI requires prompt vascular assessment, wound care and consideration of revascularisation.
Acute limb ischaemia is an emergency; UFH is commonly used while urgent revascularisation is arranged, unless contraindicated.
Do not confuse vascular-dose rivaroxaban with full-dose anticoagulation for AF or VTE.
Antithrombotic treatment after revascularisation must be individualised to the procedure, indication and bleeding risk.

blocks.text: Prescribing note: This chapter is a clinical reference, not a substitute for individual prescribing. Confirm local product labelling, renal/hepatic function, interactions and contraindications. Acute limb ischaemia and CLTI require timely vascular specialist involvement.
